profiles.meeting_scenario: At a 220-bed teaching hospital, a medical-surgical unit is starting a 6-week evaluation of bedside shift handoff using the SBAR technique to see whether it improves patient-reported quality of nursing care measured with QUALPACS. This coordination meeting takes place three days before rollout between the nurse leader responsible for implementation on the unit and the quality analyst responsible for the evaluation workflow. The agenda is to confirm the rollout timeline, which SBAR materials and observation tools will be used, how patient QUALPACS forms will be distributed and logged, and who will own the shared tracker and weekly status updates. The expected outcome is a practical division of work for training, bedside observation, patient survey collection, and reporting during the first post-implementation month.

members.name: Neda Rahimi
members.expertise: Bedside nursing workflow, staff training, SBAR handoff coaching, competency check-offs
members.background: Neda is an RN with 12 years in adult medical-surgical nursing and the last 4 years as unit educator across two inpatient floors; she has led prior bedside handoff training and is trusted by charge nurses to translate policy into practical shift routines.
members.private_state: She wants the rollout to feel manageable for bedside staff and to avoid anything that looks like extra surveillance during already tight shift changes; she is also trying to show early implementation progress to nursing leadership without reopening debates about workflow burden.
hidden_assumptions: When leadership says the unit will 'go live' on Monday, that means bedside nurses are expected to use SBAR from that date even if night-shift stragglers finish training later that week.

The 'SBAR template' for this project is the laminated bedside cue card and paper coaching guide she finalized in version 3.1 for training sessions, because that is what nurses will actually hold during handoff.
A 'completed observation' means a trained observer stands at the bedside for the full verbal handoff and checks whether all SBAR elements were spoken in front of the patient.
QUALPACS collection naturally applies to patients who directly experienced the bedside shift handoff being evaluated, not to all inpatients who happen to be on the unit that day.

members.name: Arman Salehi
members.expertise: Hospital quality measurement, patient-reported outcome collection, audit design, dashboard reporting
members.background: Arman has a master's degree in health services research and supports nursing quality projects by building data capture processes, maintaining shared trackers, and preparing reports for the quality committee and Magnet documentation.
members.private_state: He wants a clean, defensible dataset that can be summarized weekly without manual cleanup, and he is quietly trying to keep the project aligned with existing audit infrastructure so he does not have to create a separate custom monitoring process.
hidden_assumptions: The project is not really 'live' until all shifts are trained and audit entries can be counted consistently, because otherwise the baseline and post period will be contaminated.
The 'SBAR template' is the EHR handoff smartphrase and audit worksheet already stored in the quality team's SharePoint folder, since those are the artifacts that feed reports.
A 'completed observation' can be logged when the charge nurse documents the handoff audit in the routine compliance tool, even if the observer only spot-checks portions of the exchange.
QUALPACS distribution for the post-implementation period should include all eligible patients on the unit during the sampling window so the denominator stays stable across weeks.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to Monday as the unit's 'go-live' date for SBAR.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means Monday is the first day nurses are expected to perform bedside SBAR handoff on the unit, even if a few staff members finish training later in the week.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means Monday is only the operational start of the project, while post-implementation counting should begin once all shifts are trained and auditable later that week.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital rollout language, 'go-live' sounds universally understood, and both are comfortable treating Monday as the public start date while silently attaching different implications for when data should count.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will use the 'latest SBAR template' and put it in the shared folder.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the laminated bedside cue card and paper coaching sheet, version 3.1, that she uses in staff teaching and competency checks.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the EHR handoff smartphrase and accompanying audit worksheet, version 2.8, already linked to the quality team's reporting process.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Each works with a different concrete artifact but both are legitimately called the SBAR template in local practice, so the phrase creates false consensus instead of prompting clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the unit should log ten 'completed observations' per week.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes each completed observation must involve someone directly witnessing the full bedside verbal handoff with all SBAR sections delivered in front of the patient.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes an observation counts if the charge nurse enters the audit in the compliance tool for that shift, even when it is based on partial spot-checking and routine documentation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are aligned on the number and the purpose of observations, and in many hospital projects the word 'observation' loosely covers both direct witnessing and audit completion, so neither expects a standard mismatch.

misalignment_points.topic: Who is included in post-implementation QUALPACS collection
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss getting QUALPACS from 'patients on the unit after implementation.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means patients who actually experienced a bedside shift handoff during the post-rollout period, because the study is evaluating the handoff encounter itself.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means all eligible inpatients on the unit during the sampling window after rollout, regardless of whether a full bedside handoff was directly observed for them.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both framings are defensible and use the same plain-language description, and because patient survey logistics are being discussed as coordination details rather than study design decisions, the inclusion boundary stays implicit.

turns.inner_thought: Monday is the point when bedside nurses are expected to start doing SBAR at the bedside, even if a few night-shift people are still wrapping up training. I need this to sound organized and realistic, not like we're delaying again or adding a lot of burden at shift change. If Arman has the evaluation pieces lined up, we can show nursing leadership we're moving.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. From the unit side, we're in good shape for the Monday go-live for SBAR. I mostly want to make sure the implementation piece and the evaluation piece run together cleanly over this first month so staff aren't getting mixed messages.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we can treat Monday as the official start marker, but I only want the post-implementation data summarized once all shifts are trained and the entries are consistent enough to stand up on the dashboard. If I can keep this inside the existing audit structure, I won't have to invent a separate process and then clean up messy data later.
turns.utterance: That works. I have the tracker drafted for the post-implementation period starting from go-live, and my main goal is to keep the weekly numbers clean enough that I can use them for the quality dashboard without a lot of back-end fixing.

turns.inner_thought: I need everyone coaching from the laminated bedside cue card and the paper guide I finalized in version 3.1. That's what nurses will actually have in hand during report, and it's the least intimidating way to get this adopted. I'll put those materials in the folder so nobody says they didn't have the current version.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll upload the latest SBAR template along with the pocket materials today so the charge nurses on both shifts are coaching from the same language at the bedside.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then I'll point the folder to the EHR smartphrase and the audit worksheet version we already use in SharePoint. If we're all using the latest SBAR template, I can tie the reporting fields to that and avoid creating one-off categories. This should slot neatly into the audit packet.
turns.utterance: That's great. Once it's there, I'll link the latest SBAR template in the shared folder and use it for the audit packet and the reporting fields so we're all pulling from the same source.

turns.inner_thought: Ten completed observations per week feels ambitious but still manageable if I do several full bedside handoffs myself on days and have charge nurses cover some evenings. To me that means someone is actually present for the full verbal SBAR in front of the patient, otherwise it doesn't tell us whether the practice is really happening.
turns.utterance: For the observation piece, I was thinking we aim for ten completed observations per week. I can personally cover several on day shift, and the charge nurses can help on evenings so we spread it out.

turns.inner_thought: Ten a week is fine if those are just the routine compliance entries coming in from each shift. I don't need a special shadowing process as long as the charge nurses enter them promptly in the normal tool. That gives me a stable count and keeps the workload off me.
turns.utterance: Yes, ten completed observations per week sounds workable. I can pull that count from the routine compliance entries as long as each shift gets them submitted on time.

turns.inner_thought: For QUALPACS, the cleanest thing is to give it to patients who actually had the bedside report after rollout. Otherwise we're surveying people who didn't experience the handoff we're trying to improve, which won't help the unit understand whether bedside SBAR changed anything.
turns.utterance: On the patient side, the nurses can hand out QUALPACS to patients on the unit after implementation once they've had the bedside report. That should be straightforward to work into the shift routine.

turns.inner_thought: I'll structure the log around all eligible patients on the unit during the sampling window after rollout so the denominator is steady week to week. If the unit only gives surveys selectively, the data will be impossible to compare. I can say it in a way that sounds operational, not argumentative.
turns.utterance: Okay. I'll set up the survey log so we capture patients on the unit after implementation in a consistent way, which should help keep the weekly denominator steady.

turns.inner_thought: I should flag the last training detail so there are no surprises, but I don't want this to sound like a reason to push the start. A few night nurses finishing on Tuesday doesn't change that Monday is when bedside SBAR begins. Leadership will expect the practice to start then, and I don't want staff hearing that we're somehow not live yet.
turns.utterance: One small note: I still have a few night-shift nurses finishing training on Tuesday, but that shouldn't affect the go-live. The expectation on the unit is still that Monday is the start.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. I'll label Monday as go-live in the tracker for the project record, and then I'll start the weekly summary when the first full set of usable entries comes through. That way the timeline is preserved publicly, but the reported data won't be patchy from partial training or uneven observation logging.
turns.utterance: That's fine with me. I'll mark Monday as go-live in the tracker, and then I'll begin the weekly summary once the first full set of entries is in so the reporting starts off clean.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll keep ownership on the practical pieces: staff coaching, sending the bedside cue card and paper guide, reminding charge nurses they need ten real bedside observations a week, and making sure patients who got bedside handoff are offered the form. If this stays simple and concrete, staff will cooperate.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll own the staff coaching, send over the SBAR template today, and remind the charge nurses about the observation target and the patient forms so the unit side stays moving.

turns.inner_thought: And I'll lock down the infrastructure around my existing reporting process: folder structure, tracker, dashboard format, and survey log. As long as the template, completed observations, and patient surveys come in through the channels I'm expecting, I can produce a defensible weekly report without manual reconstruction.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll finalize the folder, the tracker, and the weekly report format based on the template, the completed observations, and the patient surveys we talked through today.
